title: The river bank
hookLine: a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time, says the Oankar

lines: A TREE AT THE WATER'S EDGE.
ONE DAY THE BANK LETS GO.
cards: A tree stands at the edge of a river. Its leaves are full, its shade is good, birds sit in it. From the path it looks like it will stand forever.
But down at the waterline, where nobody looks, the current is working, a little soil every day. Then one ordinary afternoon, no storm, no warning, the bank lets go and the tree leans into the water.
The Oankar, Guru Nanak's poem on the letters, stops on that picture: a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time.

teach.h: A TREE THAT CAN FALL AT ANY TIME.
teach.b: The Oankar walks through the letters, and at each one it sets down a teaching. Here the teaching is a picture: a tree standing on a riverbank, which can fall at any time. Notice what the picture doesn't say.
It doesn't say the tree is weak, or foolish, or doing anything wrong. A tree on a riverbank is just where it is.

teach.h: THE DANGER IS IN THE GROUND.
teach.b: The danger is in the ground under it, slowly being carried away. That's one way the Guru Granth Sahib speaks of a human life: not as a disaster waiting to happen, but as something standing on ground that is always moving.

teach.h: SHEIKH FARID: HOW LONG ITS FOOTING?
teach.b: The same picture shows up in the verses of Sheikh Farid, the Sufi poet whose words are also kept in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: a tree on the riverbank, how long can it keep its footing?
How long can water stay in a pot of unbaked clay? Two voices from two different worlds, one image, kept side by side in the same scripture. So what is the picture for?

teach.h: NOT FEAR: A QUESTION OF TIMING.
teach.b: In the Oankar, the shortness of life becomes a question of timing.
If the bank can give way any day, the things that matter can't wait for a safer season. The Name, the apology, the visit, the kindness you meant to get to: now is the bank you're standing on.
In Sikh teaching, that's clarity, not gloom. The current is real. So is the shade, while it lasts.

how: Sikh hymns recall how short life is, as a reason to remember the Name now; the verses of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, are sung and read with the Gurus' hymns.

o: life stands on ground that's always moving
the edge where the yogis met Nanak
a holy place to bathe and wash away sin

games.q: what's inside the river bank — tap the pairs.
p: is in the ground, not the tree
how long can it keep its footing?
how long can it hold water?

s: in the picture, the tree falls because it did something wrong
the tree is just where it is; the ground under it is being carried away.
Sheikh Farid's verses in the Guru Granth Sahib use a riverbank tree too
a tree on the riverbank, how long can it keep its footing?
the riverbank picture is meant to make life feel hopeless
it turns the shortness of life into a question of timing: what matters can't wait.

games.q: the bank under your tree is slowly washing away. what does the Guru's teaching do with that picture?
o: despair: nothing lasts, so nothing matters.
ignore it: the leaves look fine.
act now: what matters can't wait for a safer season.
games.why: the shortness of life becomes a question of timing: the Name, the kindness, the visit belong to today.

practice: Stand by water if you can, a river, a pond, even a running tap, or picture a riverbank under you, and let your attention go to your feet: the ground is taking your weight, holding today.
Stay a few breaths with the water moving and the ground holding, then let one thing come to mind that you've been putting off for a safer season, and just name it.
If you pray, remember the One beside the water; if not, let the water keep time.

wordCard.voice: The river bank. In the Oankar, a tree on the riverbank can fall at any time: life stands on moving ground, so what matters can't wait. Today's word.

orig.note: kandhi: the riverbank, as in Sheikh Farid's salok of the tree on the bank.

carryVoice: Your line: the bank gives way. What matters can't wait for a safer season. See you on the path.

sources.ref: Salok Sheikh Farid ('kandhee utai rukhrraa'), Ang 1382
